title: Detection Strategy for Dynamic API Resolution via Hash-Based Function Lookups
shortTitle: Detection Strategy for Dynamic API Resolution via Hash-Ba...
summary: This strategy addresses dynamic application programming interface resolution, where code finds a function at run time from a numeric hash instead of importing it by name. The technique matters because it removes the readable function names and import table entries that static analysis and many detections rely on, and it lets a program load only the calls it needs. Detection therefore has to come from behaviour: library load events, run time function lookup tracing and the process context that surrounds them. The usual failure is that application programming interface tracing is high volume and disabled by default, so the rule is blind unless you deliberately enable and filter it. This is independent study material and not an authoritative reference.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for programs that locate system functions in an unusual way at run time. Normally a program lists the functions it needs in a small table, and that table is easy to read. A hiding program instead asks the system for each function by a number, so the names never appear. The detection watches the requests and the libraries involved.
beginner.whyItMatters: Analysts and scanners often learn what a program does by reading its list of function names. When that list is empty or tiny, the program looks harmless and boring. Hiding the names is also a sign that the author does not want to be understood. If you cannot read the names, you must watch the behaviour instead. That is slower, so automation and good filtering matter.
howItWorks: A tracing provider records each library load and each function lookup that a process performs.
The rule flags processes that load libraries and then resolve many functions one by one in a short burst.
It compares the number of named imports in the file with the number of run time lookups, because a wide gap is suspicious.
It records the loaded library path, so function requests aimed at unusual or renamed libraries stand out.
It keeps the parent process, because a shell or an office application spawning this behaviour changes the risk.
Alerts are grouped by process so an analyst reviews one story instead of hundreds of single calls.
beginner.example: Imagine a visitor who needs tools from a workshop. A normal visitor writes a list at the front desk: hammer, saw, tape. The list is easy to read and the guard knows what to expect. A different visitor arrives, points at unlabelled drawers one at a time and takes whatever is inside. The guard never learns the plan from the list, only from watching the hands. Hash based lookups are that second visitor, and run time tracing is the guard watching the drawers.
takeaways: Hiding function names removes the easiest clue about what a program does.
Detect the behaviour of run time lookups, not the names, because the names are gone.
Run time tracing is noisy, so always count events per process and filter by parent.

objectives: Explain what a run time function lookup is and why it hides program intent.
Name the tracing and library load telemetry that can reveal the behaviour.
Set a per process count threshold that separates normal startup from a burst of lookups.
Recognise the software in your estate that resolves functions at run time for legitimate reasons.
Describe how to confirm a finding with safe static checks instead of executing the file.
dataSources: Endpoint tracing provider events for library load and exported function lookup made by a process
Sysmon event 7 image load including image path, signature status and loading process
Windows Security event 4688 process creation with command line auditing to capture the launching context
Linux eBPF or audit based tracing of dynamic symbol resolution calls in running processes
Static file metadata from a hash lookup service showing the number of entries in the import table
logic: The pattern is a process that resolves far more functions at run time than its import table declares, especially against libraries whose names do not match the process purpose. The fields to correlate are the loading process identifier and image path, the library path being queried, the count of lookup events per minute per process, and the parent image. Legitimate cases are language run times, plug in hosts, anti cheat and licence checkers, all of which resolve functions dynamically and consistently on every host in the fleet, usually with a stable library set. Malicious cases show a low import count in the file, a burst of lookups immediately after load, a library loaded from a user writable directory, and a parent such as a script interpreter or an office application. Because the volume of tracing data is large, an absolute count threshold per process plus an allowlist of known dynamic hosts keeps the rule usable.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Burst of Runtime Function Resolution by Non Standard Process
# logsource:
#   product: windows
# detection:
#   selection_trace:
#     EventID: 7
#     ImageLoaded|contains:
#       - '\\AppData\\'
#       - '\\Temp\\'
#       - '\\ProgramData\\'
#     Signed: 'false'
#   selection_lookup:
#     EventName: 'FunctionLookup'
#     LookupCount|gte: 25
#   filter_known_hosts:
#     Image|endswith:
#       - '\\python.exe'
#       - '\\javaw.exe'
#       - '\\node.exe'
#   condition: selection_trace and selection_lookup and not filter_known_hosts
# level: medium
falsePositives: Scripting language run times that resolve native functions at run time on every execution
Licence management and copy protection components that hide their own lookups as a design choice
Antivirus and endpoint agents that load plug in modules from their own program data directory
Software installers that probe for optional operating system functions before using them
Packaged internal applications that use a plugin architecture with runtime loaded modules
tuningNotes: Enable the tracing provider only on high value asset groups, because collecting it everywhere is expensive and will drown the queue. Baseline the processes that normally perform many run time lookups, then allowlist by image plus signer and by library directory, and raise the per process count threshold using the ninety fifth percentile you measure. Add a signed equals false condition to remove vendor software, and keep the parent process field in the alert so triage is fast. Narrowing this way loses detection of a signed binary that performs hidden lookups, so pair the rule with periodic import table reviews of newly seen executables in user writable paths.
